extraction_notes.note: theorem or definition: the paper presents the capacity formula as Shannon's channel coding theorem, but it serves as the definition of $C_P(N)$ here.

The general method of intersecting densities is modelled as an unmarked algorithm (a procedure with steps) rather than a claim.

nodes.name: Shannon differential entropy
nodes.statement: For a random variable $X$ with density $f$ its Shannon differential entropy is defined by the formula $h(X)=-\int f \ln f$, provided that this integral converges, with the convention that $0 \ln 0 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $h(X)=-\int f\ln f$ for a random variable with density $f$.

nodes.name: Gaussian maximizes entropy under fixed variance
nodes.statement: It is a classical fact that $h(X) \leq h(G)$ if $X$ is a random variable with finite second moment and $G$ is a Gaussian random variable satisfying $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{Var}(G)$. Thus, a Gaussian random variable maximizes entropy under a fixed variance (note that even if $X$ has finite second moment, the integral in the definition of $h(X)$ may diverge to $-\infty$, but never to $+\infty$). This statement can be rewritten in the form of a variance-entropy comparison as follows: for any random variable $X$ with finite second moment one has $h(X) \leq \frac12 \ln\left( 2\pi e \mathrm{Var}(X) \right)$, see e.g. Theorem 8.6.5 in \cite{CT06}.
assumptions: $X$ is a random variable with finite second moment
$G$ is a Gaussian random variable satisfying $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{Var}(G)$
nodes.statement_short: Among variables of fixed variance the Gaussian has maximal entropy: $h(X)\le\frac12\ln(2\pi e\,\mathrm{Var}X)$.

nodes.name: Pinsker-Csiszár-Kullback inequality
nodes.statement: Due to the Pinsker-Csisz\'ar-Kullback inequality, see \cite{P64,C62,K67}, one has $d_{\textrm{TV}}(X, G) \leq 2(h(G)-h(X))$, whenever $G$ is a Gaussian random variable with the same mean and variance as the random variable $X$. Here $d_{\textrm{TV}}$ stands for the total variation distance.
assumptions: $G$ is a Gaussian random variable with the same mean and variance as the random variable $X$
nodes.statement_short: Total variation distance to the matching Gaussian is bounded by the entropy deficit.

nodes.name: Kullback–Leibler divergence
nodes.statement: In fact, we have $D_{KL}(X \| G) = h(G)-h(X)$, where $D_{KL}$ is the so-called Kullback–Leibler divergence (or relative entropy).

nodes.name: Monotonicity of entropy in the central limit theorem (Artstein-Ball-Barthe-Naor)
nodes.statement: In the celebrated article \cite{ABBN04} Artstein, Ball, Barthe and Naor showed that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with variance $1$ and $S_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(X_1+\ldots+X_n)$, then the sequence $(h(S_n))_{n \geq 1}$ is nondecreasing.
assumptions: $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with variance $1$

nodes.name: Barron's entropic central limit theorem
nodes.statement: The convergence of this sequence to $h(G)$, where $G$ is a standard Gaussian random variable, was established much earlier by Barron in \cite{B86}, under minimal conditions that $h(S_{n_0})>-\infty$ for at least one $n_0 \ge 1$ (see also the work \cite{L59} of Linnik for some partial results).
conclusions: The convergence of this sequence to $h(G)$
nodes.statement_short: Entropy of normalized sums converges to Gaussian entropy if finite for some $n_0$.

nodes.name: Maximal entropy of weighted sums of i.i.d. random variables
nodes.statement: For a given sequence $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ of i.i.d. random variables with finite second moment find the maximum of the function \[ S_+^{n-1} \ni (a_1,\ldots, a_n) \mapsto h\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right). \] What if $S_+^{n-1}$ is replaced with $S^{n-1}$?
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $h(\sum a_iX_i)$ over unit vectors $a$ (nonnegative or arbitrary) for i.i.d. $X_i$.
nodes.label: prob:general

nodes.name: Unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ and its nonnegative part $S_+^{n-1}$
nodes.statement: Here by $S^{n-1}$ we denote the unit Euclidean sphere centered at the origin and  we take $S_+^{n-1}= S^{n-1} \cap [0,\infty)^n$.

nodes.name: Euclidean norm and scalar product notation
nodes.statement: In this article $| \cdot|$ denotes the standard Euclidean norm and $\scal{\cdot}{\cdot}$ stands for the standard scalar product in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: Equality in distribution
nodes.statement: By $\sim$ we denote equality in distribution of random variables.

nodes.name: Gamma distribution
nodes.statement: By Gamma $(\alpha, \beta)$ we mean a probability distribution admitting a density $\Gamma(\alpha)^{-1}\beta^{\alpha}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}$ on $(0, \infty)$, and in case $\beta = 1$ we abbreviate it to Gamma($\alpha$).

nodes.name: Integrals and expectations are well defined
nodes.statement: We also implicitly assume that in our abstract statements all integrals and expected values are well-defined and may have values $\pm \infty$.

nodes.name: Entropy maximality of equal weights for sums of i.i.d. Gamma variables
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be i.i.d.\ Gamma$(\alpha)$ random variables with $\alpha > 0$. Then for any integer $n\geq1/\alpha$ and any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$ one has \[ h\left( \sum_{i=1}^n d_i X_i \right) \leq h\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right), \] with equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$.
assumptions: $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be i.i.d.\ Gamma$(\alpha)$ random variables with $\alpha > 0$
any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$
conclusions: equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement_short: For $n\ge1/\alpha$, equal weights maximize the entropy of a unit-norm nonnegative weighted sum of i.i.d. Gamma($\alpha$) variables.
nodes.label: prop:diagonal-chaos

nodes.name: Entropy Schur-concavity for Gaussian mixtures (Eskenazis-Nayar-Tkocz)
nodes.statement: The only general result that we are aware of is Theorem 8 in \cite{ENT18}, where the problem was solved in the case of $X_i$ being i.i.d. Gaussian mixtures, that is, random variables of the form $X_i \sim R_i \cdot g_i$, where random variables $g_i \sim \mc{N}(0,1)$ and random variables $R_i>0$ are independent. In fact, the authors showed a stronger statement: if $X_i$ are i.i.d. Gaussian mixtures and $(a_1^2, \ldots, a_n^2) \prec (b_1^2, \ldots, b_n^2)$ in the Schur order, then $h(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i) \geq h(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i X_i)$.
also_stated_at: However, due to the result from \cite{ENT18}, if $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. Gaussian mixtures, then $a^2 \prec b^2$ implies $h(X_a) \geq h(X_b)$.
assumptions: $(a_1^2, \ldots, a_n^2) \prec (b_1^2, \ldots, b_n^2)$ in the Schur order
nodes.statement_short: For i.i.d. Gaussian mixtures, entropy of $\sum a_iX_i$ is Schur-concave in $(a_i^2)$, solving Problem 1 for them.

nodes.name: Schur order (majorization)
nodes.statement: Let us recall that the definition of the Schur order is that for vectors $(p_1, \ldots, p_n)$ and $(q_1, \ldots, q_n)$  we have $(p_1,\ldots, p_n) \prec (q_1,\ldots, q_n)$ iff $\sum_{i=1}^k p_i^\ast \leq \sum_{i=1}^k q_i^\ast$ for all $k=1,\ldots, n$ with equality for $k=n$, where $(p_i^\ast)$ and $(q_i^\ast)$ are nonincreasing rearrangements of the sequences $(p_i)$ and $(q_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: $p\prec q$ iff partial sums of decreasing rearrangements of $p$ are dominated by those of $q$, with equal totals.

nodes.name: Entropy power inequality (linearized form)
nodes.statement: The latter is, in fact, true not only for Gaussian mixtures, but for arbitrary i.i.d. random variables $X_i$, which is an easy consequence of the famous entropy power inequality of Shannon and Stam (see \cite{S48, S59}) in the following linearized form: if the real numbers $a_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$, then for a sequence of independent random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ one has $h(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i) \geq \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 h(X_i)$.
assumptions: a sequence of independent random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n$
nodes.statement_short: Linearized Shannon-Stam EPI: $h(\sum a_iX_i)\ge\sum a_i^2h(X_i)$; hence $a=e_1$ minimizes entropy in Problem 1.

nodes.name: Gaussian quadratic form
nodes.statement: Let $G_n$ be a standard $\mc{N}(0,I_n)$ Gaussian random vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($I_n$ stands for the $n \times n$ identity matrix). For a symmetric $n \times n$ real matrix $A$ we define $X_A = \scal{AG_n}{G_n}$. The random variable $X_A$ is called a \emph{Gaussian quadratic form} (in $n$ variables). If $A$ is additionally positive semi-definite, then $X_A$ is called a \emph{nonnegative Gaussian quadratic form}.
differentia: For a symmetric $n \times n$ real matrix $A$

nodes.name: Sharp variance-entropy comparison for nonnegative Gaussian quadratic forms
nodes.statement: Let $X_A$ be a nonnegative Gaussian quadratic form. Then \[ h\left( X_A \right) \leq h\left( \chi^2(n) \right) + \frac12 \ln \mathrm{Var}(X_A) - \frac12 \ln (2n) \] with equality if and only if $A= \lambda I_n$ for some $\lambda>0$. Here $\chi^2(n)= |G_n|^2$ is a random variable with a chi-square distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom. Equivalently, if $G$ is a Gaussian random variable with the same variance as $X_A$, then $h(G)-h(X_A) \geq \frac12\ln(4 \pi e n)-h(\chi^2(n)) = \frac{2}{3n} + o(1/n)$.
assumptions: $X_A$ be a nonnegative Gaussian quadratic form
conclusions: equality if and only if $A= \lambda I_n$ for some $\lambda>0$
nodes.statement_short: Among nonnegative Gaussian quadratic forms of fixed variance, $\chi^2(n)$ (scaled identity) maximizes entropy; relative entropy to Gaussian is at least $2/(3n)$.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Nonnegative quadratic forms are far from Gaussian in relative entropy
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{thm:main} shows that, in a sense of relative entropy, a Gaussian random variable cannot be approximated by a nonnegative Gaussian quadratic form too well, that is, if $\mathrm{Var}(X_A)=\mathrm{Var}(G)$, then $D(X \| G) \geq \frac{2}{3n}+o(1/n)$.
nodes.statement_short: A Gaussian cannot be approximated by a nonnegative quadratic form better than $2/(3n)$ in relative entropy.

nodes.name: Derivation of Corollary 2 from Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Since for a standard  $\mc{N}(0,1)$ Gaussian random variable $g$ its square $g^2$ has the same distribution as $2X$, where $X$ is a Gamma$(1/2)$ random variable, we get the following fact, of which Corollary \ref{thm:main} is a simple consequence.
nodes.statement_short: Since $g^2\sim 2\,$Gamma$(1/2)$, apply Theorem 1 with $\alpha=1/2$.

nodes.name: Entropy maximality of equal weights for weighted sums of squared Gaussians
nodes.statement: Let $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Then for any $n\geq 1$ and any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$ one has \[ h\left( \sum_{i=1}^n d_i g_i^2 \right) \leq h\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i^2 \right), \] with equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$.
assumptions: $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be independent standard Gaussian random variables
any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$
conclusions: equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$
nodes.statement_short: Equal weights maximize entropy of unit-norm nonnegative combinations of squared standard Gaussians.
nodes.label: cor:1

nodes.name: Derivation of Corollary 3 from Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Similarly, since Gamma$(1)$ is the same distribution as Exp($1$), we also get the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Gamma(1) = Exp(1); apply Theorem 1 with $\alpha=1$.

nodes.name: Entropy maximality of equal weights for weighted sums of exponentials
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be independent standard exponential random variables, i.e. random variables with densities $e^{-x}$ on $[0, \infty)$. Then for any $n\geq 1$ and any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$ one has \[ h\left( \sum_{i=1}^n d_i X_i \right) \leq h\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right), \] with equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$.
assumptions:
$X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be independent standard
exponential random variables
any nonnegative real numbers $d_1, \ldots, d_n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 = 1$
conclusions: equality if and only if $d_1=\ldots= d_n=1/\sqrt{n}$
nodes.label: cor:2

nodes.name: Rotation invariance of Gaussian quadratic forms
nodes.statement: Let $X_A$ be a Gaussian quadratic form in $n$ variables and let $U$ be an orthogonal transformation in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then $X_{U^\ast A U}$ has the same distribution as $X_A$. In particular, every Gaussian quadratic form has the same distribution as a certain Gaussian quadratic form with $A$ being diagonal. If additionally $X_A$ was assumed to be nonnegative, then the associated diagonal matrix has nonnegative entries.
assumptions: $X_A$ be a Gaussian quadratic form in $n$ variables
conclusions: $X_{U^\ast A U}$ has the same distribution as $X_A$
every Gaussian quadratic form has the same distribution as a certain Gaussian quadratic form with $A$ being diagonal
If additionally $X_A$ was assumed to be nonnegative, then the associated diagonal matrix has nonnegative entries
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonal conjugation preserves the law of $X_A$, so one may take $A$ diagonal (nonnegative if $A\succeq0$).
nodes.label: lem:rotation

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Let $G_n \sim \mc{N}(0,I_n)$. Note that because of rotation invariance of $G_n$, the random vector $G_n'=U G_n$ has the same distribution as $G_n$. We have $X_{U^\ast A U} = \scal{U^\ast A U G_n}{G_n} = \scal{A U G_n}{U G_n} =\scal{A G_n'}{G_n'}$, which has the same distribution as $\scal{AG_n}{G_n}=X_A$. To prove the second part it suffices to observe that every symmetric matrix is diagonalizable by a certain orthogonal change of basis $U$. If the matrix $A$ is positive semi-definite, then the resulting diagonal matrix clearly has nonnegative entries.
nodes.statement_short: Rotation invariance of $G_n$ plus orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices.

nodes.name: Introduce $G_n$ and note $UG_n$ has the same law
nodes.statement: Let $G_n \sim \mc{N}(0,I_n)$. Note that because of rotation invariance of $G_n$, the random vector $G_n'=U G_n$ has the same distribution as $G_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $G_n$ and note $UG_n$ has the same law.

nodes.name: Compute $X_{U^*AU}$ as a quadratic form in $UG_n$
nodes.statement: We have $X_{U^\ast A U} = \scal{U^\ast A U G_n}{G_n} = \scal{A U G_n}{U G_n} =\scal{A G_n'}{G_n'}$, which has the same distribution as $\scal{AG_n}{G_n}=X_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $X_{U^*AU}$ as a quadratic form in $UG_n$.

nodes.name: Diagonalize $A$ orthogonally; PSD gives nonnegative entries
nodes.statement: To prove the second part it suffices to observe that every symmetric matrix is diagonalizable by a certain orthogonal change of basis $U$. If the matrix $A$ is positive semi-definite, then the resulting diagonal matrix clearly has nonnegative entries.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize $A$ orthogonally; PSD gives nonnegative entries.

nodes.name: Mean and variance of a Gaussian quadratic form
nodes.statement: Let $X_A$ be a Gaussian quadratic form. Then $\mathbb{E} X_A = \mathrm{tr}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_A)=2\mathrm{tr}(A^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:variance

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:rotation} and by the invariance of $\mathrm{tr}(A)$ and $\mathrm{tr}(A^2)$ under matrix similarity, the statement is invariant under the transformation $A \to U^\ast A U$ for any orthogonal matrix $U$. nodes.name: Sign change point
nodes.statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable function. We say that $f$ \emph{changes sign} at point $x \in \mathbb{R}$ if one of the following conditions holds: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] there exist $y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $y < x < z$ and $f$ is positive a.e. on $(x, z)$, nonpositive a.e. on $(y, x)$ and negative on some subset of $(y, x)$ of positive measure; \item[(b)] there exist $y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $y < x < z$ and $f$ is negative a.e. on $(x, z)$, nonnegative a.e. on $(y, x)$ and positive on some subset of $(y, x)$ of positive measure. \end{itemize} We call such $x$ the \emph{sign change point} of $f$. If $f$ has precisely $n$ sign change points, then we say that $f$ \emph{changes sign exactly $n$ times}.
nodes.statement_short: $x$ is a sign change point of $f$ if $f$ switches from (a.e.) one sign to the other at $x$.

Suppose also that $U,V$ are real random variables with densities $f_U$ and $f_V$ supported in $[L,\infty)$, such that $\mathbb{E} U= \mathbb{E} V$, $\mathbb{E} U^2= \mathbb{E} V^2$, and the function $f_V-f_U$ changes sign exactly three times and is positive a.e. before the first sign change point. Then $\mathbb{E} \Phi(U) < \mathbb{E} \Phi(V)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Our goal is to prove the inequality $\int \Phi (f_V-f_U) > 0$. Because of our assumptions, we have $\int x^i f_U(x)\mathrm{d} x = \int x^i f_V(x)\mathrm{d} x$ for $i=0,1,2$. Our desired inequality is therefore equivalent to \begin{equation} \int_L^{\infty} (\Phi(x) - (a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0))(f_V(x)-f_U(x)) \mathrm{d} x > 0, \end{equation} where $a_0, a_1, a_2$ are arbitrary real numbers. A crucial step now is to explore the freedom of the choice of these three numbers. We know that $f_V-f_U$ changes sign exactly three times at some points $x_0<x_1<x_2$. We choose $a_0,a_1,a_2$ so that $\Phi(x_i)=a_2 x_i^2 + a_1 x_i+a_0$ for $i=0,1,2$. This can be done because the matrix $(x_i^j)_{i,j=0}^2$, associated to the system of linear equations that $a_0,a_1,a_2$ have to satisfy, is a $3 \times 3$ Vandermonde matrix. Let $\Psi(x)=\Phi(x) - (a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0)$. We now show that the integrand $\Psi(f_V-f_U)$ in \eqref{eq:pos-int} is nonnegative, which will clearly finish the proof (the obtained inequality will be strict because it will also easily follow that this integrand is not an a.e. zero function). We already know that $\Psi(x_0)=\Psi(x_1)=\Psi(x_2)=0$ and that $f_V-f_U$ changes sign at $x_0, x_1, x_2$ and is positive a.e. before the first sign change point $x_0$. Since close to $x=L$ the function $\Psi(x)$ is positive (note that $\lim_{x \to L^+} \Psi(x)=+\infty$), it is enough to show that $\Psi$ also changes its sign at $x_0, x_1, x_2$ and that these are the only sign change points of this function. To show this we observe that the function $\Psi$ has the form $\Psi(x)= -\tau \ln(x-L)+ax^2+bx+c$ for some real numbers $a,b,c$. This function is clearly smooth on $(L,\infty)$. It is enough to show that $\Psi$ has only three zeros and none of them is a zero of $\Psi'$ (then we easily conclude that the zeros correspond to sign changes). Suppose that $\Psi$ has more than three zeros, counting multiplicities ($x$ is a zero of multiplicity $k$ if $\Psi^{(j)}(x)=0$ for $j=0,1,\ldots, k-1$, where $\Psi^{(j)}$ is the $j$th derivative of $\Psi$, with the convention that $\Psi^{(0)}=\Psi$). Since $\Psi$ itself has at least three distinct zeros, by Rolle's theorem we deduce that $\Psi'$ has at least three distinct zeros. But for $x>L$ we have $ \Psi'(x) = \frac{-\tau}{x-L} + 2ax+b. $ Thus, the equation $\Psi'(x)=0$ is equivalent to the quadratic equation $(2 a x + b)(x-L)=\tau$, which cannot have more than two solutions (unless $\Psi'$ vanishes identically, which clearly does not hold in our case as $\tau>0$). We arrived at a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the quadratic interpolating $\Phi$ at the three sign changes; the remainder changes sign exactly there. Key step: Rolle's theorem bounds zeros of $\Psi$ since $\Psi'=0$ is quadratic.

nodes.statement: Let $\rho_{d_1, d_2}$ be the density of $d_1 X_1+ d_2 X_2$. Clearly $\rho_{d_1, d_2}$ is supported in $[0,\infty)$. nodes.statement: Since for any random variable $X$ and any real number $s$ we have $h(s+X)=h(X)$, we can replace the random variables $X_i$ with $Y_i=X_i-\mathbb{E} X_i = X_i - \alpha$. Proof can be reduced to $\alpha\in(0,1/2]$ case as sum of $k$ independent copies of Gamma$(\alpha)$ random variable follows Gamma$(k\alpha)$ distribution. Indeed, if we show that equal weights in a weighted sum of $n' = nk$ independent Gamma$(\alpha)$ random variables maximise the entropy, then the same result for the weights in a weighed sum of $n$ independent Gamma$(k\alpha)$ random variables will follow. Note that the assumption $n' \geq 1/\alpha$, needed to use the case of $n'$ summands and Gamma$(\alpha)$ random variables, is equivalent to $n \geq \frac{1}{k\alpha}$, which is the assumption for $n$ summands and Gamma$(k\alpha)$ random variables. By Lemma \ref{lem:entropy-standard-bound}(b), Lemma \ref{lem:continuity} and Lemma \ref{lem:wyrownywanie-wystarczy}, it is enough to show that \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] for $0 \leq d_1 < d_2$ satisfying $d_1^2+d_2^2 \leq 1$ one has \[ \mathbb{E} \Phi_n (s+d_1 Y_1 + d_2 Y_2) < \mathbb{E} \Phi_n \left(s+ \sqrt{(d_1^2+d_2^2)/2}(Y_1 + Y_2) \right) \] for every $s \geq -\alpha \sqrt{(n-2)(1-d_1^2-d_2^2)}$ (note that in our case $l=\alpha$), where on $(-\alpha\sqrt{n},\infty)$ we have $\Phi_n = - \ln p_n$ and $p_n$ is the density of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}( \text{Gamma}(n\alpha)-n\alpha)$, \item[(b)] there exists a measurable function $M:(-\alpha,\infty)^n \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\sup_{x \in S_+^{n-1}} |\Phi_n(\scal{x}{y})| \leq M(y)$ and $\mathbb{E} M(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n) < \infty$. \end{itemize} We first verify (a). The density $q_n$ of Gamma$(n\alpha)$ is equal to \[ q_n(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} x^{n\alpha-1} e^{-x} \mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(x), \] hence the density of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} (\text{Gamma}(n\alpha)-n\alpha)$ is equal to \begin{align*} p_n(x) & = \sqrt{n}q_n(\sqrt{n}x+n\alpha) \\ & = \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} (\sqrt{n}x+n\alpha)^{n\alpha-1} e^{-\sqrt{n}x - n\alpha} \mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(\sqrt{n}x + n\alpha) \\ & = \frac{n^{n\alpha/2}}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} (x + \alpha\sqrt{n})^{n\alpha -1} e^{-\sqrt{n}x - n\alpha} \mathbf{1}_{[-\alpha\sqrt{n},\infty)}(x). \end{align*} Therefore, for $x \geq -\alpha \sqrt{n}$ we have $ \Phi_n(x) = \left( 1 - n\alpha \right) \ln (x + \alpha\sqrt{n}) + \sqrt{n}x + c_n, $ where $c_n$ depends only on $n$. By Lemma \ref{lem:method-of-int-dens}, it is enough to show that the difference $f_V-f_U$ of the densities $f_U$ and $f_V$ of $U=s+d_1 Y_1 + d_2 Y_2$ and $V=s+\sqrt{(d_1^2+d_2^2)/2}(Y_1+Y_2)$, respectively, changes sign exactly three times and is positive a.e. before the first sign change point. This is guaranteed by Lemma \ref{lem:3-times}. Let us now show (b). The affine part of $\Phi_n$ can easily be handled, since for $x \in S_+^{n-1}$ we have $\abs{\scal{x}{y}} \leq |y|$ and $\mathbb{E} \abs{(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n)} \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}|Y_i| = n \mathbb{E} |Y_1|<\infty$. We have to bound $\abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})}$ for $y \in (-\alpha,\infty)^n$. Note that if $t \geq 1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = \ln t \leq t-1 \leq t$ and if $0<t<1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = -\ln t=b \ln (t^{-1/b}) \leq b(t^{-1/b}-1) \leq b t^{-1/b}$ for any $b>0$. Thus, $\abs{\ln t} \leq t+ b t^{-1/b}$ for every $t,b>0$ and we get \[ \abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})} \leq \abs{\scal{x}{y}} + \alpha\sqrt{n} + b (\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}. \] The term $\abs{\scal{x}{y}}$ can be bounded as above and $\alpha\sqrt{n}$ is a finite constant. We are therefore left with the term $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}$. Suppose that $ \min_i x_i \le 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$, say, $x_1 \leq 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$. Then \[ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \leq x_1 + \sqrt{n-1}(1-x_1^2) \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}} + \sqrt{n-1}. \] Define $c_n = \sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}}$. We have $c_n>\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}+ \sqrt{n}}=0$. Hence, $\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n} \geq \alpha\sqrt{n}-\alpha\sum_{i} x_i \geq \alpha c_n$, so $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b} \leq c_n^{-1/b}$, uniformly with respect to $y$. If for all $i$ we have $x_i > 1/(2\sqrt{n})$, then \begin{align*} (\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b} & \leq \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i+\alpha) \right)^{-1/b} \leq (2\sqrt{n})^{1/b} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i+\alpha) \right)^{-1/b} \\ & \leq (2\sqrt{n})^{1/b} (y_1+\alpha)^{-1/b}. \end{align*} Now we set $b=2/\alpha$. $ 
where $c_n$ depends only on $n$. By Lemma \ref{lem:method-of-int-dens}, it is enough to show that the difference $f_V-f_U$ of the densities $f_U$ and $f_V$ of $U=s+d_1 Y_1 + d_2 Y_2$ and $V=s+\sqrt{(d_1^2+d_2^2)/2}(Y_1+Y_2)$, respectively, changes sign exactly three times and is positive a.e. before the first sign change point. This is guaranteed by Lemma \ref{lem:3-times}.
nodes.statement_short: Verify (a) via Lemmas 4 and 9.

nodes.name: Compute $p_n$
nodes.statement:
We first verify (a). The density $q_n$ of Gamma$(n\alpha)$ is equal to 
\[
q_n(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} x^{n\alpha-1} e^{-x} \mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(x),
\]
 hence the density of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} (\text{Gamma}(n\alpha)-n\alpha)$ is equal to
\begin{align*}
	p_n(x) 
	  & = \sqrt{n}q_n(\sqrt{n}x+n\alpha) \\ 
	  & =  \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} (\sqrt{n}x+n\alpha)^{n\alpha-1} e^{-\sqrt{n}x - n\alpha} \mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(\sqrt{n}x + n\alpha) \\
	  & =  \frac{n^{n\alpha/2}}{\Gamma(n\alpha)} (x + \alpha\sqrt{n})^{n\alpha  -1} e^{-\sqrt{n}x - n\alpha} \mathbf{1}_{[-\alpha\sqrt{n},\infty)}(x).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $p_n$.

nodes.name: $\Phi_n$ has the form of Lemma 4
nodes.statement:
Therefore, for $x \geq -\alpha \sqrt{n}$ we have
$
	\Phi_n(x) =  \left( 1 - n\alpha \right) \ln (x + \alpha\sqrt{n}) + \sqrt{n}x  + c_n,
$ 
where $c_n$ depends only on $n$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_n$ has the form of Lemma 4.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4; sign pattern from Lemma 9
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:method-of-int-dens}, it is enough to show that the difference $f_V-f_U$ of the densities $f_U$ and $f_V$ of $U=s+d_1 Y_1 + d_2 Y_2$ and $V=s+\sqrt{(d_1^2+d_2^2)/2}(Y_1+Y_2)$, respectively, changes sign exactly three times and is positive a.e. before the first sign change point. This is guaranteed by Lemma \ref{lem:3-times}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 4; sign pattern from Lemma 9.

nodes.name: Verify (b): construct the dominating function
nodes.statement:
Let us now show (b). The affine part of $\Phi_n$ can easily be handled, since for $x \in S_+^{n-1}$ we have $\abs{\scal{x}{y}} \leq |y|$ and $\mathbb{E} \abs{(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n)} \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}|Y_i| = n \mathbb{E} |Y_1|<\infty$. We have to bound $\abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})}$ for $y \in (-\alpha,\infty)^n$. Note that if $t \geq 1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = \ln t \leq t-1 \leq t$ and if $0<t<1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = -\ln t=b \ln (t^{-1/b}) \leq b(t^{-1/b}-1) \leq b t^{-1/b}$ for any $b>0$. Thus, $\abs{\ln t} \leq t+ b t^{-1/b}$ for every $t,b>0$ and we get
\[
	\abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})} \leq \abs{\scal{x}{y}} + \alpha\sqrt{n} + b (\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}.
\]
The term $\abs{\scal{x}{y}}$ can be bounded as above and $\alpha\sqrt{n}$ is a finite constant. We are therefore left with the term $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}$. 

Suppose that  $ \min_i x_i \le 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$, say, $x_1 \leq 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$. Then 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \leq x_1 + \sqrt{n-1}(1-x_1^2) \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}} + \sqrt{n-1}. 
\] 
Define $c_n = \sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}}$. We have $c_n>\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}+ \sqrt{n}}=0$. Hence, $\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n} \geq \alpha\sqrt{n}-\alpha\sum_{i} x_i  \geq \alpha c_n$, so $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b} \leq c_n^{-1/b}$, uniformly with respect to $y$. 

If for all $i$ we have $x_i > 1/(2\sqrt{n})$, then 
\begin{align*}
  (\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b} & \leq \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i+\alpha) \right)^{-1/b} \leq (2\sqrt{n})^{1/b} \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i+\alpha) \right)^{-1/b} \\ & \leq (2\sqrt{n})^{1/b} (y_1+\alpha)^{-1/b}.
\end{align*}
Now we set $b=2/\alpha$. Since 
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}(Y_1+\alpha)^{-1/b} = \mathbb{E} X_1^{-\alpha/2} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty x^{-\alpha/2}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x}\mathrm{d} x = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha/2)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}<\infty,
\end{align*}the proof is completed.
nodes.statement_short: Verify (b): construct the dominating function.

nodes.name: Affine part is integrable
nodes.statement: Let us now show (b). The affine part of $\Phi_n$ can easily be handled, since for $x \in S_+^{n-1}$ we have $\abs{\scal{x}{y}} \leq |y|$ and $\mathbb{E} \abs{(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n)} \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}|Y_i| = n \mathbb{E} |Y_1|<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Affine part is integrable.

nodes.name: Bound $|\ln t|\le t+bt^{-1/b}$
nodes.statement:
We have to bound $\abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})}$ for $y \in (-\alpha,\infty)^n$. Note that if $t \geq 1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = \ln t \leq t-1 \leq t$ and if $0<t<1$, then $\abs{\ln t} = -\ln t=b \ln (t^{-1/b}) \leq b(t^{-1/b}-1) \leq b t^{-1/b}$ for any $b>0$. Thus, $\abs{\ln t} \leq t+ b t^{-1/b}$ for every $t,b>0$ and we get
\[
	\abs{\ln(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})} \leq \abs{\scal{x}{y}} + \alpha\sqrt{n} + b (\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}.
\]
The term $\abs{\scal{x}{y}}$ can be bounded as above and $\alpha\sqrt{n}$ is a finite constant. We are therefore left with the term $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\ln t|\le t+bt^{-1/b}$.

nodes.name: Case some $x_i$ small: uniform bound
nodes.statement:
Suppose that  $ \min_i x_i \le 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$, say, $x_1 \leq 1/(2 \sqrt{n})$. Then 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \leq x_1 + \sqrt{n-1}(1-x_1^2) \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}} + \sqrt{n-1}. 
\] 
Define $c_n = \sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{n}}$. We have $c_n>\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}- \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}+ \sqrt{n}}=0$. Hence, $\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n} \geq \alpha\sqrt{n}-\alpha\sum_{i} x_i  \geq \alpha c_n$, so $(\scal{x}{y}+\alpha\sqrt{n})^{-1/b} \leq c_n^{-1/b}$, uniformly with respect to $y$.
nodes.statement_short: Case some $x_i$ small: uniform bound.

nodes.name: Case all $x_i$ large: integrable bound with $b=2/\alpha$
nodes.statement_short: Case all $x_i$ large: integrable bound with $b=2/\alpha$.

nodes.name: Additive-noise transmission channel
nodes.statement: Consider a memoryless transmission channel with power budged $P$ subject to additive noise $N$.

nodes.name: Channel input and output
nodes.statement: If $X$ is an input of the channel then the output produced by the channel at the receiver is $Y=X+N$, where $X$ and $N$ are independent.

nodes.name: Shannon's channel coding theorem (capacity formula)
nodes.statement:
The \emph{capacity} of the channel is given by the famous channel coding theorem of Shannon (see \cite{S48}):
\[
	C_P(N) = \sup_{X: \ \mathrm{Var}(X) \leq P} (h(X+N) - h(N)).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Capacity of the additive-noise channel with power $P$ is $\sup_{\mathrm{Var}X\le P}(h(X+N)-h(N))$.

nodes.name: Noise power
nodes.statement: Let $P_N = \mathrm{Var}(N)$ be the noise power.

nodes.name: Entropy power
nodes.statement:
Shannon (see \cite{S48}, Theorem 18) gave the following bounds 
\begin{equation} \frac12 \ln\left( 1+\frac{P}{\mc{N}(N)} \right) \leq C_P(N) \leq \frac12 \ln\left( \frac{P+P_N}{\mc{N}(N)} \right),
\end{equation}
where $\mc{N}(N)=\frac{1}{2\pi e} \exp(2h(N))$ is the so-called \emph{entropy power}.

nodes.name: Shannon's capacity bounds
nodes.statement: \frac12 \ln\left( 1+\frac{P}{\mc{N}(N)} \right) \leq C_P(N) \leq \frac12 \ln\left( \frac{P+P_N}{\mc{N}(N)} \right),
nodes.statement_short: Capacity is sandwiched between $\frac12\ln(1+P/\mathcal N(N))$ and $\frac12\ln((P+P_N)/\mathcal N(N))$.
nodes.label: eq:shannon

nodes.name: Proof of Shannon's capacity bounds
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from Gaussian maximum entropy, lower bound from the entropy power inequality.

nodes.name: Right inequality via Gaussian entropy maximality
nodes.statement_short: Right inequality via Gaussian entropy maximality.

nodes.name: Left inequality via the EPI
nodes.statement_short: Left inequality via the EPI.

nodes.name: Capacity bounds for channels with gamma noise
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 1/\alpha$. The capacity of the additive channel with power budget $P$ and noise of the form $N=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, where $X_i \sim \textrm{Gamma}(\alpha)$, and with noise power $P_N$ satisfies \[ \frac12 \ln \left(1+ \frac{P}{P_N} \cdot \tau(n \alpha) \right) \leq C_P(N) \leq \frac12 \ln \left(\frac{P+P_N}{P_N }\tau(\alpha) \right) \] with \[ \tau(x)=\mc{N}(x^{-\frac12}\textrm{Gamma}(x))^{-1} = 2\pi e \exp(-2x-2 \ln \Gamma(x)-2(1-x) \psi(x)+ \ln x), \] where $\psi$ denotes the digamma function. The upper bound holds for every $n \geq 1$ and $\alpha>0$.
assumptions: noise of the form $N=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, where $X_i \sim \textrm{Gamma}(\alpha)$
conclusions: The upper bound  holds for every $n \geq 1$ and $\alpha>0$
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided capacity bounds for additive noise that is a weighted sum of $n$ i.i.d. Gamma($\alpha$) sources, via $\tau(x)$.
nodes.label: cor:capacity

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{prop:diagonal-chaos} yields \[ \mc{N}\left(|a| X_1 \right) \leq \mc{N}(N) \leq \mc{N}\left(\frac{|a|}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right). \] Note that here the lower bound is a simple consequence of the entropy power inequality (this was already mentioned in Section \ref{sec:intro}). Since $\mathbb{E} X_i=\alpha$, we have $P_N = \mathbb{E}|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(X_i-\alpha)|^2=|a|^2 \mathbb{E}|X_1-\alpha|^2=\alpha |a|^2$. Thus, due to the scaling property $\mc{N}(cX)=c^2 \mc{N}(X)$, we get \begin{align*} \mc{N}\left(\frac{|a|}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right) & = \mc{N}\left(\frac{|a|}{\sqrt{n}} \textrm{Gamma}(n\alpha) \right) \\ & = \mc{N}\left(\frac{\sqrt{P_N}}{\sqrt{n \alpha}} \textrm{Gamma}(n\alpha) \right) \\ & = P_N \mc{N}\left(\frac{\textrm{Gamma}(n\alpha)}{\sqrt{n \alpha}} \right) = P_N \tau(n \alpha)^{-1}. \end{align*} To finish the proof it suffices to use the Shannon bound \eqref{eq:shannon}.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 and the EPI sandwich the entropy power of the noise; scaling computes it, then apply Shannon's bounds.

nodes.name: Sandwich $\mathcal N(N)$ via Theorem 1 and EPI
nodes.statement:
Theorem \ref{prop:diagonal-chaos} yields
\[
\mc{N}\left(|a| X_1 \right) \leq \mc{N}(N) \leq \mc{N}\left(\frac{|a|}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right).
\]
Note that here the lower bound is a simple consequence of the entropy power inequality (this was already mentioned in Section \ref{sec:intro}).
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $\mathcal N(N)$ via Theorem 1 and EPI.

nodes.name: Compute $P_N=\alpha|a|^2$
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbb{E} X_i=\alpha$, we have $P_N = \mathbb{E}|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(X_i-\alpha)|^2=|a|^2 \mathbb{E}|X_1-\alpha|^2=\alpha |a|^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $P_N=\alpha|a|^2$.

nodes.name: Scaling gives $\mathcal N=P_N\tau(n\alpha)^{-1}$
nodes.statement_short: Scaling gives $\mathcal N=P_N\tau(n\alpha)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Plug into Shannon's bounds
nodes.statement: To finish the proof it suffices to use the Shannon bound \eqref{eq:shannon}.
nodes.statement_short: Plug into Shannon's bounds.

nodes.name: Improvement over the trivial capacity bound
nodes.statement: Since $\mc{N}(N) \leq \mathrm{Var}(N)=P_N$ one always has $C_P(N) \geq \frac12 \ln(1+\frac{P}{P_N})$ with equality for $N$ being Gaussian noise. In the proof of Corollary \ref{cor:capacity} we have used a sharper bound on $\mc{N}(N)$, and thus our result improves upon this trivial bound. It follows that $\tau(x) \geq 1$ for $x \geq 1$. In fact numerical simulations show that $\tau$ is a decreasing function of $x$ on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ as $x \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 5 improves the trivial bound $C_P\ge\frac12\ln(1+P/P_N)$; numerically $\tau$ decreases to 1.

nodes.name: Entropy maximizers for general (indefinite) Gaussian quadratic forms
nodes.statement: In this article we considered only nonnegative quadratic forms. It is natural to ask about an analog of Theorem \ref{thm:main} for general quadratic forms. This corresponds to proving an analog of Theorem \ref{prop:diagonal-chaos}, that is, maximizing $h\left(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i g_i^2\right)$ under the constraint $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2=1$, where $g_i$ are independent $\mc{N}(0,1)$ random variables. Numerical simulations show that $d_1=1/\sqrt{2}$ and $d_2=-1/\sqrt{2}$ give the maximum for $n=2$, which suggests that for general $n=2k$ a natural candidate for the maximizer would be $d_1=\ldots=d_n = -d_{n+1} = \ldots = -d_{2n}= 1/\sqrt{2n}$. We do not have any predictions in the odd case.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $h(\sum d_ig_i^2)$ over unit $d$ with signs allowed; conjectured balanced $\pm$ maximizer for even $n$.
nodes.label: que:1

nodes.name: Entropy maximizers for signed sums of exponentials
nodes.statement: Similarly to Question \ref{que:1}, we can ask about the maximum value of $h(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i X_i)$ under the constraint $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 =1$, where $X_i$ are independent standard exponential random variables, that is, random variables with densities $e^{-x}\mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(x)$. Probably the maximizers are be the same as in Question \ref{que:1}.

nodes.name: Most Gaussian direction for uniform random variables
nodes.statement: Suppose $U_1, \ldots, U_n$ are independent random variables distributed uniformly in $[-1,1]$. Is it true that $h(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i U_i) \leq h(n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n U_i)$, whenever $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2=1$?
nodes.label: que:uniform

nodes.name: Equal weights maximize entropy for symmetric log-concave variables?
nodes.statement: More ambitiously, we can ask similar questions about some larger classes of random variables. For example, suppose that $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. symmetric log-concave random variables (that is, random variables with densities of the form $e^{-V}$, where $V:\mathbb{R} \to (-\infty,\infty]$ is convex). Is it true that $h(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i X_i)$ is maximized when the coefficients $d_i$ are all equal? The answer to this question is not known even for $n=2$.

nodes.name: Is $h(X_1+X_2)\le h(X_1+G)$ for i.i.d. $X_1,X_2$?
nodes.statement: Among all random variables with a fixed variance the one maximizing the entropy is a Gaussian random variable. Suppose $X_1, X_2$ are i.i.d. and suppose that $G$ is a Gaussian random variable satisfying $\mathrm{Var}(X_1)=\mathrm{Var}(G)$. Is it always true that $h(X_1+X_2) \leq h(X_1+G)$? Let us mention that this inequality does not hold if, instead of assuming that $X_1, X_2$ are i.i.d., we only assume that they are independent with the same variances.

nodes.name: Maximal $p$th central moment of Gaussian quadratic forms
nodes.statement: Let $X_i=g_i^2-1$, where $g_i$ are i.i.d. $\mc{N}(0,1)$ random variables, and let $p>2$. What is the maximum value of $\mathbb{E}\left| \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i \right|^p$ under $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 =1$? In other words, what is the maximum possible $p$th central moment of a Gaussian quadratic form under a fixed variance?
nodes.label: que:pth-for-gauss

nodes.name: Extremal Rényi entropy of Gaussian quadratic forms
nodes.statement: For a real random variable $X$ with density $f$ we define its R\'enyi entropy of order $\alpha \in (0,\infty) \setminus \{1\}$ via the expression \[ h_\alpha(X) = h_\alpha(f) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha} \ln \left( \int f^\alpha \right). \] For $\alpha=1$ we can define $h_1 = \lim_{\alpha \to 0^+} h_\alpha(f)$, which recovers the usual entropy, that is $h_1=h$. For $\alpha=\infty$ another limiting procedure justifies the definition $h_\infty(f) = - \ln \|f\|_\infty$, where $\|\cdot \|_\infty$ denotes the essential supremum of $f$ (we shall also use the notation $M(X)=\|f\|_\infty$). For fixed $\alpha \in (0,\infty]$, what is the maximal/minimal possible R\'enyi entropy of order $\alpha$ for a Gaussian quadratic form of fixed variance? Equivalently, what is the maximum/minimum of $h_\alpha(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i g_i^2)$ under the constraint $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 =1$? We note that the case $\alpha=\infty$ gives bounds on the so-called concentration function $Q(X; \lambda) = \sup_x \mb{P}(x \leq X \leq x+\lambda)$ for Gaussian quadratic forms, which would be of independent interest in probability theory. The same questions can be asked when $g_i^2$ are replaced with arbitrary i.i.d. gamma random variables $X_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Find the max/min Rényi entropy $h_\alpha$ of a Gaussian quadratic form of fixed variance, including $\alpha=\infty$.
nodes.label: que:renyi-entropy

nodes.name: Convex order
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two real random variables. We say that $X$ is smaller than $Y$ in the \textit{convex order} (denoted $X \prec Y$) if for every convex function $\phi:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ one has $\mathbb{E} \phi(X) \leq \mathbb{E} \phi(Y)$.
differentia: for every convex function $\phi:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ one has $\mathbb{E} \phi(X) \leq \mathbb{E} \phi(Y)$

nodes.name: Marshall-Proschan Schur-convexity theorem
nodes.statement: Marshall and Proschan  in \cite{MP65} observed that if the distribution of the vector (with not necessarily independent components) $(X_1,\ldots, X_n)$ has distribution that is invariant under permuting coordinates, then for any convex function $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ the function $\Psi(a_1,\ldots, a_n) = \mathbb{E} \Phi(a_1X_1,\ldots, a_n X_n)$ is Schur convex, namely if $a,b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ are such that $a \prec b$, then $\Psi(a)\leq \Psi(b)$.
assumptions: the distribution of the vector (with not necessarily independent components) $(X_1,\ldots, X_n)$ has distribution that is invariant under permuting coordinates
conclusions: for any convex function $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ the function $\Psi(a_1,\ldots, a_n) = \mathbb{E} \Phi(a_1X_1,\ldots, a_n X_n)$ is Schur convex
nodes.statement_short: For exchangeable vectors, $a\mapsto\mathbb{E}\Phi(a_1X_1,\dots,a_nX_n)$ is Schur convex for convex $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Marshall-Proschan theorem
nodes.statement:
To see this recall (see \cite{MOA11}) that $a \prec b$ if and only if there exist nonnegative numbers $\lambda_\pi$ summing up to $1$, such that $a = \sum_{\pi} \lambda_\pi b_\pi$, where $b_{\pi}= (b_{\pi(1)},\ldots, b_{\pi(n)})$ and $\pi$ is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots, n\}$. Observe that $\Psi$ is convex (as an average of convex functions) and permutation symmetric. We thus have
\[
	\Psi(a) = \Psi\left(\sum_\pi \lambda_\pi b_\pi \right) \leq  \sum_\pi \lambda_\pi \Psi\left( b_\pi \right) = \Psi(b).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Write $a$ as a convex combination of permutations of $b$ and use convexity and symmetry of $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Recall the permutation-average characterization of majorizat
nodes.statement: To see this recall (see \cite{MOA11}) that $a \prec b$ if and only if there exist nonnegative numbers $\lambda_\pi$ summing up to $1$, such that $a = \sum_{\pi} \lambda_\pi b_\pi$, where $b_{\pi}= (b_{\pi(1)},\ldots, b_{\pi(n)})$ and $\pi$ is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots, n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the permutation-average characterization of majorization.

nodes.name: Jensen with symmetry gives $\Psi(a)\le\Psi(b)$
nodes.statement:
Observe that $\Psi$ is convex (as an average of convex functions) and permutation symmetric. We thus have
\[
	\Psi(a) = \Psi\left(\sum_\pi \lambda_\pi b_\pi \right) \leq  \sum_\pi \lambda_\pi \Psi\left( b_\pi \right) = \Psi(b).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Jensen with symmetry gives $\Psi(a)\le\Psi(b)$.

nodes.name: Majorization implies convex order of weighted sums
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\phi:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is convex and we define $X_a = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, then $a \prec b$ implies $\mathbb{E} \phi(X_a) \leq \mathbb{E} \phi(X_b)$.
also_stated_at: We conclude that if $a \prec b$, then $X_a \prec X_b$.

nodes.name: Proof that majorization implies convex order
nodes.statement: Indeed, it suffices to consider $\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)= \phi(x_1+\ldots+x_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Marshall-Proschan to $\Phi(x)=\phi(\sum x_i)$.

nodes.name: Yu's entropy comparison for log-concave variables
nodes.statement: Using the above theory Yu in \cite{Y08} showed that if $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. log-concave random variables, then for every $a,b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $a \prec b$ one has $h(X_a) \leq h(X_b)$.
assumptions: $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. log-concave random variables

nodes.name: Entropy bounds for convex combinations of i.i.d. log-concave variables
nodes.statement:
In particular, if $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1$ and $a_i \geq 0$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then 
\[
h\left( \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n   X_i \right) \leq   h\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right) \leq h\left(X_1\right).
\]
conclusions: h\left( \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n   X_i \right) \leq   h\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right) \leq h\left(X_1\right).

nodes.name: Proof of the log-concave entropy comparison
nodes.statement_short: Convex order plus log-concavity: by Lemma 3, $h(X)\le\mathbb{E}[-\ln f_Y(X)]\le\mathbb{E}[-\ln f_Y(Y)]=h(Y)$.

nodes.name: Failure of Schur-concavity of entropy for symmetric log-concave variables
nodes.statement: For example, in \cite{MNT20} it was shown that even if $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. symmetric log-concave real random variables, then $a^2 \prec b^2$ (here $a^2=(a_1^2,\ldots, a_n^2)$) does not imply $h(X_a) \geq h(X_b)$, which would be a natural conjecture based on the entropy monotonicity in the Central Limit Theorem.
assumptions: $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ are i.i.d. symmetric log-concave real random variables
conclusions: $a^2 \prec b^2$ (here $a^2=(a_1^2,\ldots, a_n^2)$) does not imply $h(X_a) \geq h(X_b)$

nodes.name: Proof of the Gaussian-mixture entropy comparison
nodes.statement:
Let us recall how convex ordering is applied in this case. Since $X_i$ are Gaussian mixtures, there exist i.i.d. positive random variables $R_i$ and independent $\mc{N}(0,1)$ random variables such that $X_i \sim R_i G_i$. Thus, 
\[
X_a = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i \sim \sum_{i=1}^n a_i R_i G_i \sim \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 R_i^2 \right)^{1/2} G_1
\]
and, in particular, $X_a$ is itself a Gaussian mixture.
This is how squares of $a_i$ are introduced in the proof. Let $f_a$ be the density of $X_a$. If we now apply Lemma \ref{lem:entropy-standard-bound}, we see that it is enough to show the inequality $\mathbb{E}[-\ln f_a(X_b)] \leq \mathbb{E}[-\ln f_a(X_a)]$. This can be rewritten as 
\[
\mathbb{E} \phi\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2 R_i^2 G_1^2 \right) \leq \mathbb{E} \phi\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 R_i^2 G_1^2 \right), 
\]
where $\phi(x) = -\ln f_a(\sqrt{x})$.  Since $f_a$ is a density of a Gaussian mixture, it is of the form $f_a(x) = \int_0^\infty e^{-x^2/2t^2} \mathrm{d} \mu(t)$ for some positive measure $\mu$, and thus $f_a(\sqrt{x}) =\int_0^\infty e^{-x/2t^2} \mathrm{d} \mu(t)$. This function is clearly log-convex (just apply H\"older's inequality). Thus, $\phi$ is concave and the result follows from the fact that $a^2 \prec b^2$ implies $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 R_i^2 G_1^2  \prec \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2 R_i^2 G_1^2$ mentioned above (note that here we only need the property that $G_1^2(R_1^2, \ldots, R_n^2)$ has distribution invariant under permutation of coordinates).
nodes.statement_short: Write $X_a$ as a Gaussian mixture, apply Lemma 3, and use concavity of $\phi=-\ln f_a(\sqrt{\cdot})$ with convex order of $\sum a_i^2R_i^2G_1^2$.

nodes.name: $X_a$ is a Gaussian mixture with scale $(\sum a_i^2R_i^2)^{1
nodes.statement:
Let us recall how convex ordering is applied in this case. Since $X_i$ are Gaussian mixtures, there exist i.i.d. positive random variables $R_i$ and independent $\mc{N}(0,1)$ random variables such that $X_i \sim R_i G_i$. Thus, 
\[
X_a = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i \sim \sum_{i=1}^n a_i R_i G_i \sim \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 R_i^2 \right)^{1/2} G_1
\]
and, in particular, $X_a$ is itself a Gaussian mixture.
nodes.statement_short: $X_a$ is a Gaussian mixture with scale $(\sum a_i^2R_i^2)^{1/2}$.

nodes.statement_short: Conclude by convex order.

nodes.name: Proschan's peakedness theorem
nodes.statement: Finally, we mention a very general fact about the comparison of distribution functions of weighted sums of i.i.d. log-concave symmetric random variables due to Proschan, see \cite{P65}: if $X_i$ are i.i.d. symmetric log-concave random variables, then $\mb{P}(X_a \geq t)$ is Schur-convex in $a$, for any fixed $t>0$.
assumptions: $X_i$ are i.i.d. symmetric log-concave random variables
conclusions: $\mb{P}(X_a \geq t)$ is Schur-convex in $a$, for any fixed $t>0$

nodes.name: Weighted sum of i.i.d. Gamma variables $X_a$
nodes.statement: Consider $X_a = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, where $X_i$ are i.i.d. Gamma($\alpha$) random variables.

nodes.name: Diaconis-Perlman unique crossing conjecture
nodes.statement: In \cite{DP90} Diaconis and Perlman conjectured that the distribution functions of $X_a$ and $X_b$ cross exactly once when $a\prec b$.
conclusions: the distribution functions of $X_a$ and $X_b$ cross exactly once

nodes.name: Yu's resolution of the unique crossing conjecture
nodes.statement: This conjecture has been verified by Yu in \cite{Y17} for gamma distributions of shape parameters $\alpha \geq 1$ and disproved for $\alpha<1$.

nodes.name: Khintchine-type moment problem for weighted sums
nodes.statement: Problem \ref{prob:general} is often considered together with its moment counterpart, namely the problem of maximizing the $p$th moment $(\mathbb{E}|S|^p)^{1/p}$ of $S=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, for $p>2$, where $X_i$ are i.i.d. symmetric random variables, under a fixed variance. The latter is equivalent to proving the Khintchine-type inequality $(\mathbb{E}|S|^p)^{1/p} \leq C (\mathbb{E}|S|^2)^{1/2}$ with the optimal constant $C$ (depending on $n$ and on the distribution of $X_1$).
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $(\mathbb{E}|\sum a_iX_i|^p)^{1/p}$ under fixed variance, i.e. the optimal Khintchine constant.

nodes.name: Hanson-Wright moment estimate for Gaussian chaos
nodes.statement:
In particular, it is known that for an arbitrary $n \times n$  matrix $A$ one has, up to absolute constants,  
\[
	\left(\mathbb{E} \left| \scal{A G_n}{G_n} - \mathbb{E} \scal{A G_n}{G_n} \right|^p \right)^{1/p} \sim \sqrt{p} \| A\|_{HS} + p \|A\|,
\]    
where $\|A\|_{HS}$ stands for the Hilbert-Schmidt norm and $\|A\|$ denotes the operator norm.

nodes.name: Hadwiger's cube slicing lower bound
nodes.statement: In \cite{H72} Hadwiger proved that $|[-\frac12, \frac12]^n \cap a^{\perp}| \geq 1$ for any $a \ne 0$, that is, the $(n-1)$-dimensional central section of the cube has volume at least $1$, with equality for $a=(1,0,\ldots,0)$.

nodes.name: Ball's cube slicing inequality
nodes.statement: Later in his celebrated work \cite{B86-ball} Ball showed that for any $a \ne 0$ one has $|[-\frac12, \frac12]^n \cap a^{\perp}| \leq \sqrt{2}$.

nodes.name: Probabilistic form of cube slicing bounds
nodes.statement: One can rephrase these results as follows: if $U_1,\ldots, U_n$ are i.i.d. random variables distributed uniformly in $[-\frac12,\frac12]$ and if $f_a$ denotes the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i$, then  $1 \leq f_a(0)\leq \sqrt{2}$ for $a \in S^{n-1}$.
assumptions: $U_1,\ldots, U_n$ are i.i.d. random variables distributed uniformly in $[-\frac12,\frac12]$
$f_a$ denotes the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i$

nodes.name: Justification of the probabilistic cube slicing form
nodes.statement: Indeed, one has $f_a(0)=|[-\frac12, \frac12]^n \cap a^{\perp}|$.
nodes.statement_short: The density at 0 equals the central section volume.

nodes.name: Cube slicing bounds in terms of $h_\infty$
nodes.statement: The quantity $f_a(0)$ is equal to $\max_{x \in \mathbb{R}} f_a(x)$, due to the log-concavity and symmetry of $f_a$. As $h_\infty(f) = -\ln \|f\|_\infty$, the above inequalities can be rewritten as $-\frac12\ln 2 \leq h_\infty(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i) \leq 0$.

nodes.name: Bobkov-Naumov-Ulyanov density maximum bounds for chi-square sums
nodes.statement:
The authors showed that for positive $d_i$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2 =1$ the following bounds on the maximum of the density of $X$ hold
\[
	\frac{c_0}{\sqrt[4]{1-\max_{i} d_i^2}} \leq M\left( \sum_{i=1}^n d_i g_i^2 \right) \leq \frac{c_1}{\sqrt[4]{1-\max_{i} d_i^2}},
\]  
where $c_0>0.013$ and $c_1<1.129$.

nodes.name: Bobkov-Chistyakov bound on the maximum of the density
nodes.statement:
Let us mention here the result of Bobkov and Chirstryakov from \cite{BC14}: if $X_i$ are independent real random variables with  $M(X_i)$ finite, then for all real numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$ one has
\[
	\frac{1}{M^2(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i)} \geq \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{M^2(X_i)}.
\] 
Here the constant $\frac12$ is best possible.

nodes.name: Constrained maximization of linear functionals
nodes.statement:
Suppose $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is connected and $\mc{F}$ is a certain class of functions. Suppose we consider functionals  of the form $\Phi(f) = \int_A gf$ for some function $g$ (here we assume integrability of $fg$ for all $f \in \mc{F}$). Let $g, g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_n$ be certain functions and let $\Phi, \Phi_1,\ldots, \Phi_n$ be corresponding functionals. Suppose our goal is to maximize $\Phi(f)$ under constraints $\Phi_i(f)=m_i$ for all $i=1,\ldots, n$. In other words, our goal is to find the quantity
\[
	M_{\mc{F}}(m_1,\ldots, m_n) = \sup \left\{\Phi(f): \ f \in \mc{F}, \ \Phi_i(f)=m_i, \ i=1, \ldots, n\right\}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $\int_A gf$ over $f\in\mathcal F$ subject to $n$ moment-type constraints $\int_A g_if=m_i$.

nodes.name: Method of intersecting densities
nodes.statement:
Suppose  that we have two functions $f,f_0$ and we would like that the inequality $\Phi(f) \leq \Phi(f_0)$ holds under constraint of the aforementioned form (for example, $f_0$ is our candidate for the maximizer in the above optimization problem).  Our inequality can be written as $\int_A g(f_0-f) \geq 0$. Usually constraints prevent us from having pointwise estimate $g(f_0-f) \geq 0$, so one has to rewrite the inequality in some way. And here comes our crucial observation: due to the constraints the inequality can equivalently be written as
\[
 	\int_A (f_0-f)\left(g- \sum_{i=1}^n a_i g_i \right) \geq 0,  
\]      
where $a_i$ are arbitrary. Now the idea is to explore our freedom of the choice of $a_i$. Suppose now that the following  conditions hold:

\begin{itemize}
\item[(I)] The function $f_0-f$ changes sign exactly $n$ times.
\item[(II)] The matrix $(g_i(x_j))_{i,j=1}^n$ is invertible for all $x_1<\ldots <x_n$. 
\item[(IIIa)] For any choice of $a_i$ the function $h=g- \sum_{i=1}^n a_i g_i$ changes sign at most $n$ times.
\item[(IIIb)] If $h$ has exactly $n$ zeros, then these zeros are sign change points. 
\end{itemize}

\noindent Then we can make the integrand of constant sign in the following way: take points $x_1<\ldots< x_n$ where $f_0-f$ changes its sign and choose $a_i$ such that $h(x_i)=0$, using solvability of the corresponding system of linear equations guaranteed by (II). Then due to (IIIb) the function $h$ changes its sign in the points $x_i$, where $f_0-f$ changes its sign, and nowhere else according to (IIIa). Thus, the integrand has a constant sign (if it is negative, then $f_0$ is the minimizer, not the maximizer). The sign of the integrand is usually easy to determine by checking it in some concrete point, or in the limit as the argument converges to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Prove $\int g(f_0-f)\ge0$ by subtracting a combination of constraint functions interpolating at the sign changes of $f_0-f$, making the integrand one-signed.

nodes.name: Log-concave moment problem
nodes.statement: In \cite{ENT18-2} in Chapter 4 the technique was used to solve the log-concave moment problem, namely to find log-concave non-increasing probability densities on $[0,\infty)$ maximizing and minimizing the integral $\int_0^\infty t^p f(t) \mathrm{d} t$ subject to constraints $\int_0^\infty t^{p_i} f(t) \mathrm{d} t = m_i$, $i=1,\ldots, n$, where $p_1<p_2<\ldots<p_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Extremize $\int t^pf$ over log-concave non-increasing densities on $[0,\infty)$ with prescribed moments.

nodes.name: Latała-Oleszkiewicz Schur-concavity of moments of uniform sums
nodes.statement: In Section 3 of \cite{ENT18-2} a simple proof of the following result of Lata{\l}a and Oleszkiewicz from \cite{LO} was given using the technique of intersecting densities: if $p \geq 2$ and $U_i$ are uniform on $[-1,1]$, then $\mathbb{E}|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i|^p$ is a Schur concave function of $(a_1^2,\ldots, a_n^2)$, whereas for $1 \leq p \leq 2$ it is Schur convex.

conclusions: $\mathbb{E}|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i|^p$ is a Schur concave function of $(a_1^2,\ldots, a_n^2)$

nodes.name: Two-variable comparison for uniform sums (Eskenazis-Nayar-Tkocz)
nodes.statement: The proof relies on the following fact (an analogue of Lemma \ref{lem:wyrownywanie-wystarczy} in the present paper): $\mathbb{E}|X_\lambda+Y|^p \leq \mathbb{E}|X_{\lambda'}+Y|^p$ for $0<\lambda<\lambda'<\frac12$ with $X_\lambda = \sqrt{\lambda}U_1+\sqrt{1-\lambda} U_2$, where $Y$ is any unimodal density.

nodes.name: Sketch of the two-variable comparison via intersecting densities
nodes.statement:
The function $g(x)=\mathbb{E}_Y|\sqrt{x}+Y|^p$ turns out to be convex (in fact, as $Y$ unimodal, it is enough to check this for $Y$ being uniform on $[-1,1]$, in which case it is a simple computation). Let $f_\lambda$ be the density of $X_\lambda$. Thus, we want to show that
\[
	\int_0^\infty g(x^2)(f_{\lambda'}(x)-f_{\lambda}(x)) \mathrm{d} x \geq 0.
\]
This can be rewritten as 
\[
	\int_0^\infty (g(x^2)-(a_1+a_2 x^2))(f_{\lambda'}(x)-f_{\lambda}(x)) \mathrm{d} x \geq 0.
\]
Now assumption (I) is straightforward to verify and (III) follows from the fact that $g(t)=a_1+a_2t$ has at most two solution due to convexity of $g$.
nodes.statement_short: Convexity of $g$ plus intersecting densities with two constraints: check (I) and (III).

nodes.name: Intersecting densities for the most Gaussian direction in the cube
nodes.statement: Suppose we want to show that the maximum of $h(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i)$ for $U_i$ uniform on $[-1,1]$, under the constraint $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$, is given by $a_i=n^{-1/2}$. Then we can follow the strategy of the present paper (see Lemma \ref{lem:entropy-standard-bound}) and then proceed as in the proof of the result of Lata{\l}a and Oleszkiewicz \cite{L06}, in order to show that $\mathbb{E} \Phi_n(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i U_i) \leq \mathbb{E} \Phi_n(n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n U_i)$, where $\Phi_n= -\ln p_n$, with $p_n$ being the density of $n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n U_i$, that is, an affine image of the Irwin-Hall distribution. Here verifying (I) is the same as in the proof for moments. However, (III) is now a difficult technical problem. One can check that it would be enough to show that $(\ln p_n(x))'''\leq 0$ for $x>0$. Numerical simulations show that this is indeed true for $n \geq 7$.

nodes.statement_short: For uniform variables the method reduces to $(\ln p_n)'''\le0$ (Irwin-Hall), verified numerically for $n\ge7$.

nodes.name: Intersecting densities for $c_pe^{-|x|^p}$ Khintchine inequalities
nodes.statement: Suppose $Y_1,\ldots, Y_n$ are i.i.d. random variables with densities of the form $c_pe^{-|x|^p}$ for $p \geq 2$. In this case an analogue of the result of Lata{\l}a and Oleszkiewicz should hold. In fact, checking condition (III) is precisely the same as in the above proof. The only  problem is to verify (I), which is  technically difficult, since the density $f_\lambda$ of $X_\lambda = \sqrt{\lambda} Y_1 + \sqrt{1-\lambda} Y_2$ is now given by a complicated expression and finding the number of sign changes of $f_\lambda - f_{\lambda'}$ turns out to be challenging.
nodes.statement_short: For $c_pe^{-|x|^p}$ densities, condition (III) is as before but counting sign changes (I) is hard.
